units.english: Every high honor here in the world is surrounded by dangers: the greater the worldly dignities are, the fiercer the dangers are.
units.analysis: The two swā clauses correlate the degree of dignity and danger. The noun ār means honor or rank in this context, not a modern ethical good.

units.english: Thus we can recognize and understand the examples from this.
units.analysis: Ðā bȳsena is the accusative object of both infinitives; be ðǣm supplies an anaphoric connection. The precise idiomatic English for this connection should be reconciled with the lexical/frame audit.

units.english: The tree, then, which grows in the woodland so that it rises above all the other trees and spreads itself out—when a storm and the strong wind suddenly arise, it is more violently shaken and battered than the rest of the forest.
units.analysis: The opening tree is resumed by hit. Storm and se stranga wind are coordinated subjects of gestęnt, despite its singular form. The later ðonne is comparative; se ōðer wudu means the rest of the forest.

units.english: It is likewise with the high cliffs and crags: when they tower far above the rest of the earth, they then suddenly begin to fall and crash violently to the earth.
units.analysis: Hīe refers to the cliffs and crags. Both feallan and hrēosan depend on onginnað. Cook's probable crag interpretation of torr remains explicitly qualified.

units.english: Likewise with the high mountains and hills which stand high above all the earth: nevertheless they suffer the penalty of that supremacy, in that they are often assailed and afflicted by fire from heaven and struck with flames.
units.analysis: The dative opening phrase is followed by a resumed understood mountain/hill subject in habbað. Ðæs ealdordōmes depends on wīte. The ðæt clause explains the penalty; the final passive participle joins the pair before it. Precise rendering of the supplied participles awaits lexical checking.

units.english: Thus the high powers here in the world collapse and fall and come to ruin, and the riches of this world turn to sorrow, and these earthly wonders come to nothing.
units.analysis: The three subjects are ðā hēan mihta, ðisse worulde welan and ðās eorðlican wundor. The final noun is neuter plural. The repeated weorðað plus tō expresses three outcomes.

unresolved_points: Idiomatic force of be ðǣm in the metadiscursive sentence, preserving ðā bȳsena as the object.
Exact lexical senses of the supplied mountain passive participles; retain the three coordinated predicates.
